title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single sampled initial LLM candidate (declared model gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs analysed after preregistered exclusions. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. The exact McNemar test was the preregistered primary decision procedure (preregistration manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891); the paired bootstrap CI reported below is a supplementary/descriptive interval estimator (paired bootstrap B=10,000, seed=1729) and not used to overturn the preregistered hypothesis decision. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair was invoked in 6 episodes; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and thus could not be evaluated. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We archive exact paired counts, provider/stage accounting, representative repair diagnostics, and reconciliation artifacts to support audit and reanalysis.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→CLI translation and automated configuration synthesis [1,2]. Stochastic LLM outputs can violate syntactic and semantic constraints (missing required commands, unsafe ordering, forbidden field touches), creating operational risk when applied directly. A pragmatic mitigation pattern is generate–verify–repair (GVR): generate a candidate, deterministically verify it against an oracle (e.g., Batfish‑style checks), and, if necessary, use a bounded repair loop to correct verifier‑reported defects [3]. Prior work proposes GVR architectures and documents verifier components for NetOps, but preregistered, paired experiments that quantify verifier‑triggered repair benefit on reproducible intent→CLI task banks remain limited.

This study tests the preregistered question (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1): does a GVR pipeline that uses a single sampled initial LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), a deterministic Batfish‑style validator, and at most one automated LLM repair call reduce deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures relative to scoring the identical initial candidate without repair? Our principal contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation (planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs analysed) that reports exact paired counts, the preregistered exact McNemar decision result, a supplementary paired bootstrap CI, provider/stage accounting, representative repair diagnostics, and a focused limitations discussion grounded in archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and benchmark efforts demonstrate both opportunity and risk of LLMs in NetOps. NetConfEval‑style benchmarks evaluate intent→CLI translation and show vendor dialects, sequencing, and implicit constraints remain failure points for unconstrained generation [1]. Surveys synthesize common failure modes (hallucination, constraint violations, brittle prompts) and recommend grounding, verifier integration, or tool‑augmentation to reduce risk [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed and analyzed in code generation and regulated‑output domains as a way to combine stochastic generation with deterministic acceptance criteria [3]. Deterministic NetOps verifiers (Batfish and header‑space analyses) provide automatable reachability and policy checks but have finite rule coverage that affects measured outcomes [4]. Prior empirical work on what LLMs need to synthesize correct configurations emphasizes explicit sequencing and vendor handling, motivating verifier‑driven repair when first‑pass outputs omit constraints [5]. Our study differs by executing a preregistered, shared_initial_candidate paired test, archiving validator traces for every episode, and reporting exact contingency counts together with the preregistered hypothesis test and supplementary interval estimates.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment followed preregistration cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under these semantics a single sampled initial model candidate per task (shared across arms) is produced; baseline is the validator score on that candidate and guarded is the final validator score after the permitted bounded repair (≤1 repair call) if the shared initial candidate failed. This design isolates the incremental effect of a verifier‑triggered repair for the observed initial sample. The exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05) on paired binary outcomes was preregistered as the primary hypothesis test and decision rule; the paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) is reported as a supplementary, descriptive interval estimator and was not used to alter the preregistered decision.

Task bank, sampling, and inclusion rules: The preregistered task bank produced 300 deterministically seeded intent→CLI pairs stratified into two vendor clusters (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like). Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms). Inclusion/exclusion and contamination rules followed the preregistration: exact public duplicates would be excluded from the primary analysis (none were excluded for exact duplication), transient provider/API failures triggered up to two automatic retries, and pairs where both arms failed due to infrastructure/provider errors were excluded from the primary paired analysis per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' missingness rule. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts record planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 532, failed_episode_count = 68, and complete_pair_count = 266 (both‑arm failures excluded = 34); these exact reconciliation counts are archived (analysis deterministic_reconciliation artifact SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490).

Model orchestration, provider accounting, and semantics clarification: The declared model for all generation and any repair calls is recorded as gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Provider/stage accounting (from the execution audit) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 6, and condition_counts: shared = 300, guarded = 6. To avoid misinterpretation we explicitly define these fields as used in the evidence bundle: (a) 'shared_initial_generation' = the single sampled initial model call executed once per task whose sampled candidate is used for both the baseline and guarded outcome evaluations (this is the meaning of shared_initial_candidate semantics); (b) 'repair' = additional model calls invoked only when the shared initial candidate failed the deterministic validator; (c) the reported 'condition_counts' in the provider audit reflect model‑call stage tallies (i.e., number of model calls attributed to each stage) and do not indicate independent full‑generation calls per arm. The provider accounting therefore documents that every task had one shared initial generation (300 shared calls) and only 6 additional repair calls were made across the run.

Deterministic validator and scoring: The binary oracle deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies an archived rule battery per episode: CLI syntactic parsing/normalization, required_sequence checks, constrained_field touch checks vs allowed_touched_fields, and reachability/constraint checks over a deterministic synthetic topology (a Batfish‑style evaluation). Each episode archives validation_before and validation_after objects (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, normalized_configuration, and boolean valid). The confirmatory scoring rule for the primary binary endpoint was 'full_intent_constraint_validation' as recorded in per‑episode scorer artifacts; these per‑episode decisions produce the paired contingency used in the primary test.

Repair loop bounding and prompt construction: The repair stage was strictly bounded to at most one LLM repair call per episode. Repair prompts are archived: they include the task constraints, validator failure diagnostics, and explicit instructions to produce a corrected configuration that satisfies the same task constraints. Stage accounting indicates 6 repair calls; repair prompts and repaired outputs are archived for each invocation.

Analysis procedures: The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (α=0.05). Interval estimation used a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) for descriptive uncertainty. Missingness handling followed the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule: pairs with both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures (both_missing_pairs = 34) were excluded from the primary McNemar test; a preregistered sensitivity analysis that treats excluded episodes conservatively as failures was executed and reported. Secondary estimands (median repair iterations, median latency) were preregistered; per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be evaluated.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and sample flow: Planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 532, failed episodes = 68; after applying the preregistered missingness rule ('complete_pair_primary') complete pairs analysed = 266 (both‑arm failures excluded = 34). Provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 6. These exact accounting values are recorded in the reconciliation artifacts and analysis logs (see deterministic_reconciliation SHA above).

Primary paired outcomes: For the 266 complete pairs the paired contingency counts are n11 = 260 (both baseline and guarded pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). These yield baseline_success_rate = 260/266 = 0.9774436090 and guarded_success_rate = 265/266 = 0.9962406015; paired difference = 0.01879699248. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 5, n01 = 0) gives p = 0.0625, which does not meet the preregistered α = 0.05 reject rule.

Supplementary interval estimate and bootstrap parameters: As a descriptive supplement we computed a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) for the paired difference: 95% CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. We emphasize that this CI is supplementary and not the preregistered decision instrument; the preregistered McNemar test is the primary inferential procedure (manifest SHA‑256 cited above).

Repair invocation yield and representative diagnostics: Repair was invoked in 6 episodes (stage_counts repair = 6). At most five of those repair invocations contributed to the observed guarded‑only successes (n10 = 5) among the analysed pairs; provider accounting (repair = 6) and contingency counts (n10 = 5) are consistent and archived. Median repair iterations per analysed pair = 0. Representative repaired case: task-000008 (difficulty labeled "extreme") illustrates a typical repair scenario from the archived artifacts—its shared initial candidate lacked a completed final token line (truncated "interface uplink2\n"), causing parsed_command_count < required_command_count and triggering repair; the repair call completed the truncated command and produced the required sequence so that the guarded final validator trace shows validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0. Per‑episode validator traces for each repaired episode (validator_before/after, violation codes, normalized_configuration) are archived and permit detailed failure‑mode inspection; these per‑episode artifacts are the source for the representative diagnostics reported here.

Sensitivity to preregistered missingness handling: Excluding 34 both‑arm failed episodes yields analysed complete_pairs = 266 and the McNemar p reported above. A preregistered conservative sensitivity analysis that treats the 34 excluded both‑arm episodes as failures (complete N = 300) produces first‑pass proportions baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333; discordant counts among the complete pairs remain n10 = 5, n01 = 0 and the exact McNemar p on the analysed pairs is unchanged (p = 0.0625). This sensitivity check shows the preregistered decision outcome is robust to the conservative missingness treatment while absolute per‑condition rates change when failures are treated as losses.

Derived descriptive scalar: Given the absolute paired difference, a descriptive number‑needed‑to‑treat (NNT) analog is 1 / 0.01879699248 ≈ 53.2, i.e., under the observed conditions roughly 53 guarded tasks were associated with one additional verifier‑approved configuration relative to baseline. This NNT is a descriptive operational scalar conditional on the high baseline pass rate and shared_initial_candidate semantics and should be interpreted accordingly.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The guarded pipeline produced a small absolute improvement (~1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI (supplementary) excludes zero, illustrating finite‑sample discreteness: with few discordants (n10 + n01 = 5) McNemar’s discrete two‑sided p can be conservative while bootstrap resampling can produce a CI excluding zero. We therefore report both the preregistered decision result (primary) and the supplementary CI so readers can evaluate effect magnitude alongside formal hypothesis testing.

Operational implications and boundary conditions grounded in artifacts: Baseline first‑pass accuracy was very high (≈97.7%), so repair opportunities were rare (6/300) and marginal yield per repair was small. Provider/stage accounting shows repair overhead was limited in this run, but per‑episode timing was not archived and end‑to‑end latency could not be assessed. GVR’s marginal benefit will be larger on corpora or deployments with substantially lower first‑pass accuracy or where validator coverage catches common failure modes. Validator coverage itself is finite and determines which failures are observable and correctable; unmeasured semantics outside the validator battery remain a risk.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate the effect of validator‑triggered repair for a fixed sampled candidate but do not address alternative interventions (multiple independent draws, constrained first‑pass prompts). Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite archived rule battery; semantic violations outside that battery are unmeasured. External validity: task corpus is a seeded synthetic generator supplemented by NetConfEval‑style items and limited to two vendor dialect clusters; generalization to other vendors, larger topologies, or production heterogeneity is not established. Conclusion validity: loss of 34 both‑arm provider failures reduced effective N and produced few discordants, limiting power for small effect detection.

Design recommendations supported by execution artifacts: (1) When baseline pass rates are high, power can be increased by evaluating tasks with lower baseline accuracy or by including independent multi‑draw initial‑generation arms in the preregistration. (2) Instrument and archive per‑episode timing to evaluate latency estimands; our run lacked per‑episode timing and could not evaluate the preregistered latency bound. (3) Expand and publish validator rule coverage and include adversarial tests for verifier false negatives; per‑episode validator traces permit such audits and should be included in future preregistrations. (4) Compare shared_initial_candidate semantics to independent initial draws in separate preregistered arms if the research question requires measuring constrained‑prompt or prompt‑engineering effects; those alternative arms were not executed here.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment evaluating a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved verifier pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a supplementary paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be assessed. All raw responses, validator traces, provider accounting, and reconciliation artifacts are archived to enable audit, reanalysis, and targeted follow‑on experiments that evaluate alternative generation semantics or lower‑baseline corpora.

Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration manifest: cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Human role and autonomy boundary: before the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the autonomy lock the registered pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI‑peer review simulation, and revision. Nondeterminism disclosure: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) and no deterministic sampling seed for provider calls; therefore nondeterministic sampling of model outputs cannot be excluded for the recorded provider calls (provider audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed = 272, failed = 34; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 6). Execution and analysis artifacts, logs, and hash manifests (including deterministic_reconciliation.json and analysis artifacts) are archived in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration manifest SHA above.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule (deterministic_reconciliation.json archived; SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490), reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.
Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
Latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
